case_study_insert.main_stem: Coastal Reclaim Aggregates (CRA) is a cooperative in the demolition-waste recycling sector near Rotterdam, employing a workforce of 60 member-workers. Established in 2011 by a group of contractors led by Anouk de Vries, it supplies reclaimed aggregate to road contractors and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. CRA plans to invest $840,000 in a mobile recycling crusher and eco-screening plant, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and $340,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $264,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a tonne and a selling price of $9.20, and produces 110,000 units a year. CRA faces contamination in incoming demolition waste and the defect rate for off-specification reclaimed aggregate has reached 3.6%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The recycling line processed 27,500 tonnes last quarter, with a 3.6% off-specification rate caused by contamination, down from 4.9% a year earlier. Complaints from road contractors about dirty aggregate fell from 22 to 11 per month. Average lorry queue time is 35 minutes. Market research of 450 contractors found that 66% would pay up to $0.45 more per tonne for screened, low-contamination reclaimed aggregate, and 61% check recycled-content documentation before tendering. A skills audit shows 18 of 60 member-workers have not been trained on the new eco-screening plant; accredited courses at the regional college cost $920 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Coastal Reclaim Aggregates for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.50% to 4.25%, increasing costs for firms with variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills at labour-intensive recycling sites. (3) Wholesale diesel, crusher wear-part and transport costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, construction-cost inflation is 4.7%, and regional demolition activity grew 3.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: CRA funded its $840,000 crusher with a $500,000 bank loan and $340,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for CRA of using $340,000 retained profit rather than another share issue from its members.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no repayments or interest, so CRA avoids adding to the debt service on its $500,000 ten-year bank loan. With fixed costs of $264,000 a year and only a $4.40 contribution on each tonne, keeping cash in the cooperative protects the 60 member-workers' returns and can fund screening improvements to cut the 3.6% contamination defect rate.

Point 2: Using retained profit does not dilute members' ownership or require further capital calls from the cooperative, preserving the flat, democratic structure led by Anouk de Vries. A new share issue would ask members for more money and could create disputes about control, whereas retained profit is already available and can be applied flexibly, for example to the $920 accredited courses for the 18 untrained workers, without approaching outside investors. This matters because a cooperative relies on member confidence: keeping the $840,000 plant funded from $340,000 of past profits avoids asking the 60 members for fresh capital while the 3.6% defect rate is still being reduced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to CRA's cooperative structure, financing and operating data.

questions.question_text: CRA wants more road contractors to buy its screened reclaimed aggregate. Consider a road-building trade fair, trade-press advertising, or a direct mailshot to contractors. Which should CRA choose to promote the new eco-screening plant? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Road-building trade fair: A trade fair lets CRA show screened samples and recycled-content documents to the 61% of 450 surveyed contractors who check such paperwork, and staff can explain how contamination is reduced from 4.9% to 3.6%. Face-to-face contact builds trust with the buyers who fell to 11 complaints a month. However, stand costs and staff time are high for a cooperative committing $840,000 to new plant, and the audience is geographically limited.

Trade-press advertising: adverts in road-construction titles reach the right specialist readers at moderate cost and leave a durable record of the $0.45 premium story. The drawback is passivity: advertisers cannot answer technical questions about screening or demonstrate the plant, and response rates are hard to measure against the 27,500-tonne quarterly target.

Direct mailshot: A targeted mailing to contractors combines low cost with precise addressing of the exact buyers already surveyed, and can include a sample certificate and a clear message about low-contamination aggregate. It is measurable through replies and can be followed up personally. Its limits are a relatively low response rate and the need for an up-to-date mailing list.

Recommendation: CRA should choose the direct mailshot. It is affordable for a cooperative, precisely targets the contractors who value the $0.45 premium, and produces measurable enquiries to fill the 110,000-tonne output. The trade fair is rejected as too expensive and geographically narrow; trade press is rejected as passive and unable to demonstrate quality. CRA can support the mailshot with a small trade-press notice once responses are known.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to CRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CRA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CRA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the trade fair and trade press are rejected.

questions.question_text: CRA is a cooperative with a flat structure and democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for CRA of this leadership approach when tackling contamination and the 11 monthly complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 60 member-workers vote on how the new eco-screening plant is run, so those who see incoming demolition waste first can propose practical sorting rules. Because members own the cooperative, participation strengthens commitment to the $840,000 investment and helps reduce the 3.6% off-specification rate that caused 11 complaints a month.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens communication lines between Anouk de Vries and the 18 workers needing training, so problems with the $920 accredited courses or the 35-minute lorry queue can be raised and solved quickly. Shared decisions build trust among members, supporting the 66% of surveyed contractors who would pay $0.45 more when everyone is responsible for consistent screened quality across the 27,500 tonnes dispatched last quarter. Because members both own and work at CRA, open discussion can also surface practical sorting ideas that an autocratic manager might miss, speeding the fall from 22 to 11 complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CRA's cooperative structure, complaints, training and output.

questions.question_text: CRA wants to cut the 3.6% contamination rate among its 60 member-workers. Consider a bonus paid for clean screened loads or profit sharing across the cooperative. Which should CRA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Bonus for clean screened loads: A bonus tied to the 3.6% off-specification rate gives members a direct financial incentive to spot contamination, which should reduce the 11 monthly complaints and protect the $0.45 premium. It is easy to link to the 27,500 tonnes processed last quarter and rewards the 42 trained workers. The risks are that members might rush screening to earn the bonus, or that arguments over grading could arise, and no bonus amount can be quantified because the insert gives none.

Profit sharing: Distributing a share of profits to all 60 members suits a cooperative's democratic tradition and encourages everyone to care about quality, falling defects and the $840,000 plant's profitability. It also supports the 18 members needing $920 courses because the whole team benefits from cooperation. However, profit sharing is delayed and diluted across many members, so the link between an individual's screening effort and reward is weak, and it pays out even if contamination remains high.

Decision: CRA should choose a bonus for clean screened loads. It targets the exact 3.6% problem and gives an immediate, measurable incentive across the 27,500-tonne operation. Profit sharing is rejected because its reward is indirect and spread too thinly to change daily screening behaviour; it can be introduced later as a general reward once the defect rate is under control. A clean-load bonus is also affordable because it rewards only verified improvements in the 27,500-tonne quarterly output, whereas profit sharing would spread any gain across all 60 members regardless of who reduced contamination.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivators with limited application to CRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both motivators in the context of CRA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivators with a well-justified decision covering incentives, fairness and the defect problem.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CRA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $264,000 ÷ ($9.20 − $4.80) = $264,000 ÷ $4.40 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 tonnes a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.20 − $4.80 = $4.40. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CRA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 60,000-tonne break-even output with 110,000 tonnes produced to show a margin of safety of 50,000 tonnes before the $840,000 eco-screening plant is at risk.
2. Use the $4.40 contribution to value the $0.45 premium: if all 110,000 tonnes gained it, contribution would rise to $4.85, showing how important the 66% of survey respondents are.
3. Set repayment targets for the $500,000 bank loan: each tonne above 60,000 adds $4.40, so about 5,000 tonnes a month above break-even is needed to cover the $264,000 annual fixed costs.
4. Track unit cost ($264,000 ÷ 110,000 units + $4.80 = $7.20 a tonne) against the 3.6% contamination rate and the 8.9% diesel and wear-part inflation in Appendix 3 to spot waste early.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 tonnes | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.40 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 110,000 tonnes; valuing the $0.45 premium on $4.40 contribution; loan-service targets on $264,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.20 for contamination and inflation control.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CRA's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has CRA's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit 1,470 ÷ revenue 4,200 × 100 = 35.0% in 2024; 1,920 ÷ 4,800 × 100 = 40.0% in 2025. Operating profit 504 ÷ revenue 4,200 × 100 = 12.0%; 720 ÷ 4,800 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit 504 ÷ capital employed 2,800 × 100 = 18.0%; 720 ÷ 3,200 × 100 = 22.5%. Revenue rose from 4,200 to 4,800 while cost of sales increased from 2,730 to 2,880, so gross profit grew from 1,470 to 1,920. Capital employed rose from 2,800 to 3,200 as the $840,000 plant was commissioned, and interest expense increased from 56 to 64.

Evaluation: All three measures moved favourably, so the improvement is consistent. The wider gap between revenue and cost of sales fits the 66% of contractors who would pay $0.45 more for screened aggregate, and operating profit grew faster than revenue, showing control of overheads despite higher interest. Returns on the enlarged capital base also improved, encouraging for a newly installed crusher. Caution is needed: the 3.6% contamination defect rate and 8.9% diesel and wear-part inflation could raise costs in the next period, and the $920 training gap among 18 members may limit efficiency.

Conclusion: CRA's profitability has improved. Gross and operating margins and returns on capital all rose together, so the judgement is robust; management should secure the $0.45 premium and reduce contamination to protect it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures with little or no accurate calculation of the three measures.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CRA of its eco-screening plant producing low-contamination reclaimed aggregate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research shows 66% of 450 contractors would pay up to $0.45 more for screened, low-contamination aggregate and 61% check recycled-content documents. Eco-screening supports that premium, raising contribution from $4.40 toward $4.85 per tonne and helping the 110,000-tonne output justify the $840,000 plant. It also cuts the 3.6% defect rate and the 11 monthly complaints, strengthening CRA's reputation with road contractors.

Disadvantage: Screening adds operating cost and may not remove all contamination from variable demolition waste, so the 3.6% off-specification rate may persist, especially while 18 of 60 members lack training. Extra processing raises the $4.80 variable cost and needs the $920 courses to be effective; if contractors refuse the $0.45 premium because 8.9% diesel and transport inflation makes them price-sensitive, the higher cost would squeeze rather than improve margins. The cooperative must decide whether the $0.45 premium is secure enough to justify the extra screening cost on all 110,000 tonnes while 18 members remain untrained.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CRA's research data, costs and defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in input costs will affect CRA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.50% to 4.25%): If CRA's $500,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point increase adds 0.0075 × $500,000 = $3,750 a year (derivation shown). That is modest against $264,000 of fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher borrowing costs could still affect future finance for the $840,000 plant, though 3.2% growth in demolition activity supports demand.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, from $12.60 to $13.49 per hour): CRA employs a workforce of 60 at labour-intensive recycling sites, so the rise lifts wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay, so an annual wage figure cannot be calculated honestly; the correct approach is qualitative, judged against labour productivity of 110,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,833.3 units per worker (arithmetic shown from insert figures). If 18 members remain untrained and productivity falls, unit labour costs will rise and cut the $4.40 contribution from $9.20 less $4.80.

Input cost inflation (8.9%): The insert does not decompose the $4.80 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound can be derived: if the whole of it rose 8.9%, that is 0.089 × $4.80 = $0.4272, about $0.43 a tonne; across 110,000 tonnes this is 110,000 × $0.4272 = $46,992 a year. Even a partial pass-through reduces contribution, and 4.7% construction-cost inflation limits recovery, though the $0.45 premium accepted by 66% of contractors offers some protection.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats on all 110,000 tonnes and directly erodes the $4.40 contribution that supports the $840,000 investment, while the interest effect is a conditional $3,750 and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity. CRA should secure the premium and renegotiate diesel and wear-part supply.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to CRA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on CRA's costs or financing in context with shown arithmetic where figures are used.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context, with derivations shown and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
